title: Nicodemus, New Birth, and God's Love for the World
summary: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and leader, comes to Jesus at night, and Jesus tells him that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or from above, of water and the Spirit. Jesus speaks of the Son of Man lifted up like the bronze snake in the wilderness, and the chapter declares that God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son. John the Baptist then tells his disciples that he must decrease while Jesus increases.
story: Chapter 2 ended with many in Jerusalem believing because of Jesus' signs and with Jesus knowing what was in them. Nicodemus is one of those impressed by the signs, and his conversation shows that admiration is not yet life. The chapter moves from a private dialogue to a public declaration, then back to John the Baptist, whose ministry overlaps with Jesus' for a time. It is the first of John's long conversations, and it states themes that will run through the whole Gospel: new birth by the Spirit, eternal life, belief and unbelief, light and darkness, and the lifting up of the Son of Man. Nicodemus disappears without a clear response, but he will return in 7:50 to defend Jesus and in 19:39 to help bury him.
historical:
The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law of Moses and the traditions that interpreted it. They were respected by many ordinary Jews and believed in the resurrection and in angels. Nicodemus is also a leader of the Jews, probably a member of the Sanhedrin, the governing council in Jerusalem, and Jesus calls him Israel's teacher, suggesting a recognized scholar. His name was Greek, which was not unusual among Jews of the period.

John the Baptist's baptism was a once-for-all washing that signified repentance in preparation for the coming one. Aenon near Salim (the name Aenon means springs) cannot be located with certainty; proposals include sites in the Jordan valley and in Samaria. John notes that the Baptist had not yet been imprisoned, a detail that suggests the author expected readers to know from other accounts that Herod Antipas would later arrest him. The mention of Jesus and his disciples baptizing is clarified in 4:2, which says the disciples did the baptizing.
cultural:
Coming at night may reflect caution about being seen with Jesus, or simply the custom of rabbis studying late; John, who uses darkness and light as symbols, likely intends the reader to notice that Nicodemus comes out of the dark toward the Light. His confused question about entering his mother's womb shows that he takes Jesus literally. The phrase born of water and the Spirit would have recalled Ezekiel 36:25-27 for a teacher of Israel, where God promises to sprinkle clean water on his people and put a new spirit within them. In Hebrew and Greek the same word means wind, breath, and spirit, which gives Jesus' saying about the wind blowing where it wishes a double sense.

The bronze snake story (Numbers 21:4-9) was familiar: when the Israelites were bitten by venomous snakes in the wilderness, God told Moses to set a bronze snake on a pole, and anyone who looked at it lived. John the Baptist's image of the friend of the bridegroom draws on wedding custom, where a close friend of the groom helped arrange the wedding and rejoiced to hear the groom's voice with the bride. The Old Testament often pictures God as Israel's husband, so the Baptist is saying Jesus is the bridegroom of God's people.
literary: The chapter has two main parts, each with a dialogue followed by a reflective discourse: Jesus and Nicodemus (verses 1 to 21) and John the Baptist and his disciples (verses 22 to 36). The first conversation turns on a double meaning. The Greek word anōthen can mean again or from above, and Nicodemus hears again, while Jesus means from above, a birth that comes from God. Ancient Greek manuscripts did not use quotation marks, and interpreters disagree on where Jesus' words end and the Gospel writer's reflection begins, most often at verse 15 or verse 21. The same question arises at verse 30 or 31 with the Baptist's words. Either way, the words carry the Gospel's authority. The structure moves from misunderstanding (verses 4 and 9) to revelation, and Nicodemus's voice fades away as the discourse grows.

outline.t: Heavenly things and the Son of Man lifted up
God's love for the world; light and darkness
John the Baptist: he must increase
The one from above and eternal life

doctrines.note: “For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.” Salvation begins in God's love, is given in the Son, is received by believing, and results in eternal life rather than perishing. God's purpose in sending the Son was to save, not to condemn.

New birth is the work of the Spirit, who like the wind cannot be controlled or predicted. No one can see or enter the kingdom by effort, heritage, or religious standing. Christians differ on how baptism relates to this birth, but all agree that it is God's work, not ours.

The chapter uses believe again and again. To believe in the Son is to have eternal life; to reject him is to remain under God's wrath. Believing is compared to the Israelites looking at the bronze snake: a trusting look at what God has provided.

Judgment is described not only as a future verdict but as something already happening: people love darkness because their deeds are evil and refuse the light. The Son did not come to condemn, but rejecting him leaves a person under the condemnation that already stands.

words.note: Anōthen, from above or again. Both meanings are possible, and John uses the ambiguity. Nicodemus hears a second physical birth; Jesus means a new birth from God above, which is also a second birth. In 3:31 the same word clearly means from above, which supports that sense as primary here.

Kosmos, world. In John the word usually means humanity, often humanity organized in opposition to God, rather than the physical universe. That God so loved the world is remarkable precisely because the world did not recognize him (1:10). The greatness of God's love is measured not by the world's size but by its hostility.

Agapaō, to love. God so loved: the Greek word translated so (houtōs) means in this way more than to such a degree, so the verse describes how God loved, by giving his Son. The same verb appears in verse 19 for people who loved the darkness and in verse 35 for the Father's love for the Son.

Hupsoō, to lift up, to exalt. The Son of Man must be lifted up as the snake was. John uses the word with a double meaning: Jesus will be physically lifted up on the cross (12:32-33), and that lifting up will be his exaltation and glory.

christ: This chapter tells who Jesus is and why he came. He is the Son of Man who came down from heaven and will return there, the only one who can speak of heavenly things from firsthand knowledge. He is God's one and only Son, given by the Father's love. He must be lifted up, as the bronze snake was, so that those who look to him in faith may live. The comparison is precise: in Numbers the people were dying under judgment for their sin, and God provided the means of healing on a pole. Jesus applies that pattern to his own crucifixion. He is also the bridegroom whose coming makes John's joy complete. And he has received the Spirit without limit, and the Father has placed all things in his hands.

hard.q: Does John 3:16 mean God loves every person, and what happens to those who never believe?
hard.a: The verse speaks of God's love for the world, and in John that word most naturally means humanity in its rebellion, not a select group. Christians agree that God's love is the source of salvation and that the offer is to everyone who believes. They differ on a second-order question: whether God's saving intention in sending the Son extends equally to every person, as Arminian and Wesleyan traditions teach, or whether his love for the world is expressed in a special saving purpose for those he has chosen, as Reformed traditions teach, while still extending a sincere offer to all. Both traditions read verse 16 carefully and affirm that whoever believes will be saved. On the question of those who do not believe, the chapter is sober: whoever does not believe has already been condemned, and the wrath of God remains on them (verse 36). The Son did not bring that condemnation; he came to save from it. The chapter does not address those who never heard of Jesus, and Christians hold a range of views about them; the text's own emphasis is on the urgency of believing for those who have.

questions: Nicodemus was respected, learned, and religious, yet Jesus told him he needed to be born from above. Why might religious people find that hardest to hear?
John 3:16 says God loved the world by giving. How does knowing how God loved change the way you understand love?
John the Baptist said, “He must increase; I must decrease.” Where in your life is that exchange hardest to make?
